passages.happening:
Abimelech, Gideon's son by his concubine in Shechem, goes to his mother's family there. He tells them to ask the leaders of Shechem whether it is better to be ruled by seventy sons of Gideon or by one man, and to remember that he is their own flesh and blood (verses 1-2). The leaders are won over. “He is our brother” (verse 3).

They give him seventy shekels of silver from the temple of Baal-berith, and with it he hires worthless and reckless men to follow him (verse 4).

“He went to his father’s house in Ophrah, and on one stone murdered his seventy brothers, the sons of Jerubbaal. But Jotham, the youngest son of Jerubbaal, survived, because he hid himself” (verse 5).

Then the leaders of Shechem gather beside the oak at the pillar in Shechem and make Abimelech their king (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 8 ended with Gideon refusing a crown, naming this son with a word for king, and Israel turning to Baal-berith. This chapter shows where that led.

It is the one long story in the middle of the book with no foreign enemy, no cry to the LORD and no deliverer. The enemy is inside Israel, and the violence is between brothers and neighbors. It is also Israel's first try at having a king, and it is a disaster.

Shechem, between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim, was an old Canaanite city with a long history before Israel came, and it seems to have kept a mixed population loyal to Baal-berith, Baal of the covenant. Abimelech appeals to the loyalty that counted most in that world, family and clan: he is their own flesh and blood.

Money from a temple paid for his campaign. Religion and power were bound tightly together, and the temple of Baal pays for the murder of Gideon's sons.

Killing rival heirs was a common way for ancient rulers to make their power safe. That the seventy were killed ‘on one stone’ suggests a public execution. It is told in one sentence, and the sentence is enough. One child survives by hiding.
passages.later:
The first murder in the Bible was a brother killing a brother, and God said to Cain, “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to Me from the ground” (Genesis 4:10). This chapter will show that blood crying out too.

The story was remembered long afterwards. When one of David's soldiers died close to a city wall, Joab expected the king to ask, “Who was the one to strike Abimelech son of Jerubbesheth?” (2 Samuel 11:21).
passages.hard:
Why does the Bible tell of a massacre like this?

It tells it because it happened, and because it shows what the book is about. A son of a judge became a murderer of his own family, paid for by the temple of a false god, and the leaders of a town made him king for it. The narrator does not soften it. Later in the chapter he says plainly that God repaid Abimelech for murdering his seventy brothers, and brought the wickedness of Shechem's leaders back on their heads (verses 56-57).

The book presents none of this as a pattern. It records a massacre in order to condemn it, and the whole chapter is the working out of that condemnation.
passages.asks: Abimelech won the leaders of Shechem with an appeal to kinship. Ask how loyalty to your own group, your family, your party, your church, could lead you to back something you know is wrong. And ask whose silence you have bought, or sold, with the plea that someone belongs to your side.

passages.happening:
Jotham, the one brother who escaped, climbs Mount Gerizim and calls down to the leaders of Shechem (verse 7).

He tells a story. The trees set out to anoint a king. They ask the olive tree, the fig tree and the grapevine in turn. Each refuses. Should it give up its oil, its sweet fruit or its wine, ‘to hold sway over the trees’? (verses 8-13). At last the trees ask the thornbush. “If you really are anointing me as king over you, come and find refuge in my shade. But if not, may fire come out of the thornbush and consume the cedars of Lebanon” (verse 15).

Then Jotham applies it. If they have dealt faithfully with Gideon's house, may they and Abimelech enjoy each other. “But if not, may fire come from Abimelech and consume the leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo, and may fire come from the leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo and consume Abimelech” (verse 20).

Then he runs away and lives at a place called Beer, afraid of his brother (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Stories in which plants or animals speak were known in the ancient Near East, and Jotham's is one of the few in the Bible.

The olive, the fig and the vine were the most valued plants of the land. They gave oil, fruit and wine. Each of them is too busy being useful to want to rule. The thornbush, or bramble, is the only one that says yes. It could offer no real shade, and in the dry season it caught fire easily and spread the flames to the forest.

The point is sharp. Abimelech is a thornbush. He promises protection he cannot give, and the only thing he can really offer is fire.

The fable stands at the center of the chapter, and it tells the reader how to read everything after it. Jotham's curse is a condition: if they have acted in good faith, fine; if not, fire from each side will burn the other. The rest of the chapter is that fire.

Mount Gerizim rises over Shechem. When Israel entered the land, half the tribes had stood before it, as Moses commanded, to speak God's good words over the people. Now a lone survivor stands on it and speaks a curse.
passages.later:
Another fable of a thornbush appears centuries later, when a king of Israel warns a king of Judah: “A thistle in Lebanon sent a message to a cedar in Lebanon” (2 Kings 14:9).

Moses had commanded that when Israel crossed the Jordan, certain tribes ‘shall stand on Mount Gerizim to bless the people’ (Deuteronomy 27:12), and under Joshua they did (Joshua 8:33).
passages.asks: In Jotham's fable the good trees were too busy bearing fruit to rule, and the worthless one wanted the crown. Ask what that says about power and the people who seek it, in your town, your work or your church. And ask whether you are more eager to be in charge than to be useful.

passages.t: Three years, and a spirit of ill will
passages.happening:
Abimelech rules over Israel for three years (verse 22). Then “God sent a spirit of animosity between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem and caused them to treat Abimelech deceitfully” (verse 23). It happens so that the crime against Gideon's seventy sons might come to justice, and their blood be avenged on Abimelech and on the leaders who helped him (verse 24).

The leaders of Shechem set ambushes on the hilltops and rob travelers (verse 25). A man named Gaal moves into the city with his brothers, and the leaders trust him. At a harvest festival in the house of their god they curse Abimelech, and Gaal boasts that he would get rid of him (verses 26-29).

Zebul, the governor of the city, secretly warns Abimelech (verses 30-33). Abimelech comes by night with his troops. In the morning Gaal sees men coming down from the hills, and Zebul mocks him: “The shadows of the mountains look like men to you” (verse 36). Then he taunts Gaal to go out and fight the men he had scorned. Gaal fights, loses and is driven out of the city (verses 38-41).
passages.hearers:
The narrator never calls Abimelech a judge. He ‘reigned over Israel’ (verse 22). He is a different kind of ruler.

God has not been mentioned since the start of the chapter. Now he acts, and the way he acts is to send division between two guilty partners. Verse 24 gives the reason: the blood of the seventy must come to justice.

The leaders of Shechem are, in Hebrew, the baals of Shechem. The word means lords or owners, and it is the same word as the name of the god whose temple paid for the murders. The city's lords and its god share a name.

Gaal appeals to ‘the men of Hamor, the father of Shechem’ (verse 28). That recalls the old Canaanite ruling family of Shechem in Genesis 34, and it suggests local loyalties that were not Israelite.

The scene with Gaal and Zebul is almost comic. Gaal boasts at a feast. In the morning he sees an army coming and Zebul tells him he is looking at shadows. Then the shadows arrive.
passages.later:
Similar words are used of King Saul: “After the Spirit of the LORD had departed from Saul, a spirit of distress from the LORD began to torment him” (1 Samuel 16:14).

The old ruling family of Shechem is the one met in Genesis: “Shechem son of Hamor the Hivite, the prince of the region” (Genesis 34:2).
passages.hard:
What does it mean that God sent a spirit of animosity between Abimelech and Shechem?

The Hebrew says, literally, an evil or harmful spirit. Similar language is used when a harmful spirit from God troubles Saul.

Readers understand it in more than one way. Some take it as a personal spiritual being, sent or allowed by God as an agent of judgment. Others read it as a way of describing a mood of hostility and distrust that God allowed to grow between two guilty parties.

On either view, the text's point is the same. God is sovereign over the working out of judgment. He did not cause the murders, but he made sure the guilty did not get away with them (verse 24). And the evil was already there in both parties. God's act exposed it and turned it back on them.
passages.asks: Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem had made a partnership in murder, and it could not hold. Ask what partnerships in your own life rest on something wrong that both sides would rather not name. And ask whether you believe that God sees the blood that others have forgotten.

passages.t: Shechem destroyed, and the millstone at Thebez
passages.happening:
The next day Abimelech ambushes the people of Shechem in the fields. He fights against the city all day, captures it, kills its people, tears it down and sows it with salt (verses 42-45).

The leaders in the tower of Shechem take refuge in the inner chamber of the temple of El-berith (verse 46). Abimelech cuts a branch from the trees on Mount Zalmon, and his men do the same. They pile the branches against the chamber and set it on fire, ‘killing everyone in the tower of Shechem, about a thousand men and women’ (verse 49).

Then he attacks the town of Thebez and takes it, but its people shut themselves in a strong tower. As Abimelech comes close to the door to burn it, “a woman dropped an upper millstone on Abimelech’s head, crushing his skull” (verse 53). He calls his armor-bearer to kill him with a sword, so that no one can say a woman killed him, and the young man does (verse 54). The Israelites who followed him go home (verse 55).

“In this way God repaid the wickedness that Abimelech had done to his father in murdering his seventy brothers. And God also brought all the wickedness of the men of Shechem back upon their own heads. So the curse of Jotham son of Jerubbaal came upon them” (verses 56-57).
passages.hearers:
Jotham's curse comes true in every part. Fire comes out of Abimelech and burns the leaders of Shechem. Then fire, or the attempt at it, brings about his own death.

The chapter is full of such echoes. Seventy brothers were killed on one stone, and Abimelech is killed by one stone. He burned the tower of Shechem, and he dies trying to burn the tower of Thebez.

Sowing a city with salt was a curse, marking a place as barren and not to be lived in. The upper millstone was a heavy hand stone that women used every day to grind grain, and it was heavy enough to kill. For a warrior, death at a woman's hand was thought shameful, and so Abimelech has his armor-bearer finish him. Even in dying he thinks of his name.

The burning of the tower, with about a thousand men and women inside, is told plainly and without delight. It is the work of the man who made himself king, done to the people who made him king.

The last two verses give the narrator's own verdict, and it is one of the clearest in the book. God repaid both Abimelech and Shechem. Evil came home.

At Shechem excavators found a great fortress-temple from before Israel's time. Some connect it with the temple of El-berith and the tower of this chapter, but that link is debated.
passages.later:
The principle of these verses runs through Scripture: “He who digs a pit will fall into it, and he who rolls a stone will have it roll back on him” (Proverbs 26:27); “His trouble recoils on himself, and his violence falls on his own head” (Psalm 7:16).

David's general Joab remembered how Abimelech died: “Was it not a woman who dropped an upper millstone on him from the wall, so that he died in Thebez?” (2 Samuel 11:21).
passages.asks: Abimelech died worrying about what people would say of him. Ask what you are protecting when you guard your reputation, and whether it has cost others more than you know. And sit with verse 56. Ask whether it comforts you or frightens you that God brings evil home, and what that means for the evil you have done.
